newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Prudential reaches settlement with Florida. [CORRECTED 23:53 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. Prudential reaches settlement with Florida. [CORRECTED 23:53 GMT]

text.p: Florida's Department of Insurance said it has reached a multi-million dollar agreement in principle with Prudential Insurance Co of America to settle allegations the insurer used deceptive tactics to sell life insurance.
A news conference to discuss the settlement is scheduled for 1430 EST/1930 GMT at the insurance department's offices.
Additional details were not immediately available.
State Treasurer and Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson will be joined at the news conference at the Capitol conference room in Tallahassee by Attorney General Bob Butterworth.
Florida has been one of the most outspokent critics of Prudential's proposed class-action settlement of consumer sales complaints.
In December, Florida, along with three other states, urged a federal judge to reject Prudential's class-action settlement, calling it unfair to consumers.

Under the settlement, reached in September, Prudential agreed to pay at least $410 million to as many as 10.7 million policyholders, who bought permanent life insurance policies between 1982 and 1995. (Corrects from "between 1982 and 1985.")
The proposed settlement could cost Prudential as much as $1.2 billion in direct expenses and could have a total value to policyholders of almost $2 billion.
A hearing to determine the fairness of the proposed settlement is scheduled to begin Monday in U.S. district court in Newark, N.J.
Other states that have opposed the settlement include Massachusetts, Texas and California.
Prudential agreed late last week to pay $384,200 to settle a lawsuit brought by Virginia and it acknowledged tht some policyholders may have been misled by Prudential agents.
But Florida has been one of the staunchest critics of the settlement.
In early December, Florida's Nelson charged Prudential with obstructing a state probe into allegations that the company misrepresented its insurance policies as investments.
The commissioner at that time threatened that if the company did not provide requested documents, it could face sanctions, possibly including the los of its license to operate in Florida.
Florida attorney general Bob Butterworth also had been investigating the company to ensure that policyholders were fairly compensated.
